problem.title: Card-fraud scoring service
problem.context: A payments company scores every card transaction for fraud before it is authorized. It processes about 3,000 transactions per second on a normal day and up to five times as many during seasonal sales. Fraudsters adapt within weeks, and the confirmed fraud labels (chargebacks) arrive days to weeks after the transaction. Auditors and the card schemes can ask, months later, why a given transaction was scored the way it was. The ML team has five data scientists and two ML engineers. The company's operations team runs the data centres and the shared infrastructure, but there is no platform team for machine learning.

requirements.text: Score every card transaction before the authorization decision, using the cardholder's recent activity (for example, the spending of the last hour and the last day).
Update the model as new confirmed fraud cases arrive.
For any past score, show which model version and which input values produced it.
During a seasonal peak of 15,000 transactions per second, a score comes back within 30 ms at the 99th percentile.
When the scoring service or one of its data sources fails, authorizations go on. The business accepts weaker fraud detection for up to 15 minutes, but no authorization may fail because of scoring.
An auditor asks about a score from up to 13 months ago. Within one working day the team answers with the model version, the input values and the training data that model was built from.
When the fraud loss rate rises in one segment, a retrained model can be in production within 48 hours, after it has been compared with the current model on recent transactions.
Card data must stay inside the company's PCI-certified environment: no external service may process it.
Seven people build and run the system, with no dedicated ML platform team.

values: Scoring path: Synchronous REST on Kubernetes
Score explanation: Top three contributing features
Audit record: Append-only full input and model log
Retraining pipeline: Airflow nightly on 90 days of labels
Experiment and promotion: Three-day shadow and manual review
Monitoring: Grafana score drift and fallback dashboards
points.description: Streaming per-card aggregates are maintained in Redis and served to a synchronous REST scorer on Kubernetes, using an XGBoost model that returns a score and its top three contributing features. Failures invoke a rule engine; full inputs and model logs are appended to 13-month on-premises object storage, while Airflow retrains nightly on 90 days of labels, MLflow manages versions, three-day shadow/manual review controls promotion, and Grafana tracks drift and fallback use. Trade-off: This gains low-latency, explainable scoring, auditability, and controlled promotion, but requires consistent streaming/Redis state and costly on-premises logging and storage. The limited training window and nightly cadence may miss longer-term or rapidly changing fraud patterns.

A streaming pipeline continuously updates per-card aggregate features as card events arrive. The fraud scorer reads those current aggregates from Redis as online features when evaluating a transaction. Trade-off: This provides fresh, low-latency feature access, but relies on Redis’s in-memory availability and operational capacity, with weaker durability or historical access than a persistent feature store.

values: Scoring path: Synchronous REST on Kubernetes
points.description: A Kubernetes-hosted REST service synchronously receives each transaction and scores it with an XGBoost gradient-boosted-tree model before returning a result. If the model path fails or is unavailable, the service applies its rule-engine fallback and returns that decision instead. Trade-off: This combines immediate responses, flexible model-based scoring, and degraded-service operation, but synchronous serving can increase request latency or capacity pressure, while fallback decisions may be less accurate or consistent with the model.

values: Audit record: Append-only full input and model log
points.description: The service writes each scoring request’s full input and model log to an append-only audit record. These records are retained for 13 months in an on-premises object store, providing a historical trail for review and investigation. Trade-off: This improves auditability and supports retrospective fraud analysis, but consumes substantial storage and preserves potentially sensitive inputs for 13 months, increasing access-control and data-governance obligations.

values: Retraining pipeline: Airflow nightly on 90 days of labels
Experiment and promotion: Three-day shadow and manual review
points.description: Airflow nightly retrains the fraud model using the most recent 90 days of labels and records the resulting versions in MLflow. A candidate model spends three days in shadow mode, after which a reviewer decides whether to promote it. Trade-off: This provides repeatable retraining, version tracking, and a cautious promotion gate, but it delays adoption by the nightly schedule, three-day evaluation, and manual review. The fixed 90-day window may also limit adaptation to older patterns or longer-term drift.

values: Feature state: Batch recomputation of recent card aggregates
points.description: A batch job periodically recomputes aggregates for recent card activity and writes the resulting values to Redis. The fraud-scoring service reads those Redis aggregates during online authorization decisions. Trade-off: This provides fast online access and allows aggregate correction or rebuilding through recomputation, but values can be stale between batch runs and recomputation may create periodic processing load.

values: Scoring path: Synchronous REST on Kubernetes
Failure behavior: No fallback on scoring failure
points.description: The service exposes a synchronous REST endpoint on Kubernetes, invokes an XGBoost model for each request, and returns the fraud score in the response. If scoring fails, the request fails rather than being handled by an alternate mechanism. Trade-off: This provides direct, consistent decisions from a deployable and potentially scalable model-serving path, but makes request latency and availability depend on the scoring service and model. With no fallback, transient failures can block transactions rather than allowing degraded processing.

values: Experiment and promotion: One-day shadow and manual review
points.description: The candidate model is registered and versioned in MLflow, then deployed for one day in shadow mode alongside the live fraud system. Its scores do not affect approvals or declines; reviewers inspect selected cases manually and use those observations to decide whether to promote the registered version. Trade-off: This reduces production risk and provides a controlled human check, while preserving model lineage. It gives up immediate automated impact and requires reviewer time; a single day may also provide limited evidence about behavior across varied fraud patterns.

tradeoffs.note: These choices give fresh online features, a continuity path, retained evidence, and in-environment model operations, while the collection of streaming, serving, storage, and ML components adds operating work for a small team.

trajectory.observation: The design addresses scoring, delayed labels, replayable inputs, on-premises operation, and fail-open authorization. Its design is latency-oriented but the stated 30 ms p99 at 15,000 TPS has no benchmark evidence here. Its three-day shadow period directly conflicts with the 48-hour adaptation target. The 13-month records include model version and inputs, while MLflow's training snapshot supplies training-data lineage. The component set also creates a real burden under the small-team constraint.

trajectory.hypothesis: R1 calls for fresh per-card recent-activity features at scoring time, and Q1 favors keeping feature access fast.

tradeoffs.note: Continuously maintained online aggregates make recent activity available to the scorer, while Redis access latency and stream load still need measurement against the p99 target.

trajectory.observation: The feature choices directly provide the recent hour/day activity R1 needs, and streaming state is more current than periodic recomputation. The point is latency-oriented, but no measured result proves 30 ms at peak; that lack of evidence is an open verification question rather than a demonstrated failure.

values: Scoring path: Synchronous REST on Kubernetes
trajectory.hypothesis: R1 and Q1 call for a prompt per-transaction score, while Q2 requires authorization to continue through scoring failures.

values: Scoring path: Synchronous REST on Kubernetes
tradeoffs.note: Synchronous serving makes the model result available before authorization and a rule fallback preserves continuity, but the request path adds a latency dependency and the 25 ms timeout does not itself establish a 30 ms p99 at peak.

trajectory.observation: The fallback is directly supported by Q2's explicit acceptance of weaker fraud detection during failures. The scoring architecture is plausible for synchronous decisions, but latency capacity at the seasonal peak remains unverified.

values: Audit record: Append-only full input and model log
trajectory.hypothesis: R3 and Q3 require retrospective model/input evidence, and C1 requires that card data remain within the PCI environment.
trajectory.observation: The record captures every score's model version and complete inputs, and the retention period matches the 13-month lookback. On-premises storage keeps card data in the company's environment. MLflow's recorded training snapshot complements the score log for Q3's training-data question.

values: Retraining pipeline: Airflow nightly on 90 days of labels
Experiment and promotion: Three-day shadow and manual review
trajectory.hypothesis: R2 and Q4 call for regular retraining on arriving chargebacks, comparison against the current model, and timely production promotion; C2 favors using manageable shared tooling.

values: Retraining pipeline: Airflow nightly on 90 days of labels
Experiment and promotion: Three-day shadow and manual review
tradeoffs.note: Nightly Airflow training consumes new labels and MLflow retains model lineage, but waiting through three shadow days misses the 48-hour target. Standard tools avoid building a bespoke platform, though the pipeline and manual reviews still demand team effort.

trajectory.observation: The model is retrained daily as labels arrive and the comparison is performed, but three days of shadowing make the 48-hour production requirement impossible even before review time. The standard registry helps a small team, while the overall workflow still requires sustained operations.

values: Feature state: Batch recomputation of recent card aggregates
trajectory.hypothesis: Does R1 force streaming updates, or could periodically recomputed aggregates serve the recent-activity requirement?
trajectory.observation: Periodic recomputation can provide aggregates, but cannot ensure the freshest per-card state for every transaction and adds a stale interval before scoring. Streaming is therefore the better-supported choice for the recent-activity and low-latency intent. The exact p99 target remains unproven for either design.

values: Scoring path: Synchronous REST on Kubernetes
Failure behavior: No fallback on scoring failure
trajectory.hypothesis: Does Q2 force the rule-engine fallback when synchronous scoring fails?
trajectory.observation: Without fallback, a service timeout or outage can stop authorization, which Q2 prohibits. The rule-engine fallback is forced by Q2, while its weaker fraud detection is an accepted degradation for a bounded interval.

values: Experiment and promotion: One-day shadow and manual review
trajectory.hypothesis: Does Q4 require the three-day shadow, or can comparison and manual review be completed with a one-day shadow?

values: Experiment and promotion: One-day shadow and manual review
tradeoffs.note: A one-day shadow plus review can complete comparison within 48 hours, though the manual gate still takes scarce team time and one day may provide less evidence.

trajectory.observation: The shorter shadow preserves a recent-transaction comparison and can meet the time bound, so the three-day duration is not forced by Q4. The requirements do not establish that one day supplies enough statistical confidence; the chosen three days may be a freely chosen caution, but it misses the explicit deadline.

regions.name: Fresh online card features
regions.reason: Streaming updates and Redis lookups provide the recent per-card activity the score needs and favor low-latency reads. Peak p99 performance remains to be measured.

regions.name: Replayable score evidence
values: Audit record: Append-only full input and model log
regions.reason: The complete versioned input record retained for the requested period supports historical explanation, and on-premises storage respects the data boundary.

regions.name: Fail-open authorization
values: Scoring path: Synchronous REST on Kubernetes
regions.reason: Synchronous serving supplies a score before authorization, and the rule fallback is required to keep authorization moving during scoring failures. The model family is an implementation choice without a demonstrated requirement forcing it.

alternatives.name: Fraud scoring as built
alternatives.summary: An on-premises streaming feature and synchronous model-scoring service with a rules fallback, retained score evidence, and a nightly human-reviewed model release process.

choices.reason: Recent card activity is required at each score, and batch recomputation leaves a stale interval; the exact latency target still needs measurement.
choices.solution_quote: Flink jobs consume the topic and keep per-card aggregates (spend and counts over the last hour, day and week, and the number of distinct merchants) up to date in a Redis cluster.

choices.reason: Redis provides online access to the fresh aggregates. The requirements support low-latency feature access but do not uniquely require Redis over another in-environment online store.
choices.solution_quote: Flink jobs consume the topic and keep per-card aggregates (spend and counts over the last hour, day and week, and the number of distinct merchants) up to date in a Redis cluster.

choices.value_id: Scoring path: Synchronous REST on Kubernetes
choices.reason: A synchronous response fits scoring before authorization and Kubernetes offers a deployable serving path, but neither the interface nor runtime is uniquely required by the given requirements.
choices.solution_quote: The model is packaged in a container with a small Python REST service and runs on the company's Kubernetes cluster, with six replicas and autoscaling on CPU.

choices.reason: Q2 explicitly forbids scoring failures from stopping authorization. The contrast without a fallback misses that requirement.
choices.solution_quote: If the call times out or fails, the switch uses the existing rule engine for that transaction and logs that no score was used.

choices.reason: The model produces transaction scores and is a plausible low-latency choice, but the requirements specify no model family and no alternative was evaluated.
choices.solution_quote: The model is a gradient-boosted tree model (XGBoost).

choices.value_id: Score explanation: Top three contributing features
choices.reason: Returning influential features helps explain declines, but R3 and Q3 are principally addressed by the versioned full-input record; the exact top-three presentation is not forced.
choices.solution_quote: The service returns, with every score, the three features that pushed the score up the most, which the dispute team uses to explain declines to cardholders.

choices.value_id: Audit record: Append-only full input and model log
choices.reason: Historical explanation needs the model version and actual input values for each score; retaining only aggregate statistics would not suffice.
choices.solution_quote: Every score is written, with the model version and all input values, to an append-only table in the company's on-premises object store, kept for 13 months.

choices.reason: The record retention matches Q3's maximum lookback, and local object storage keeps card data within the PCI environment.
choices.solution_quote: Every score is written, with the model version and all input values, to an append-only table in the company's on-premises object store, kept for 13 months.

choices.value_id: Retraining pipeline: Airflow nightly on 90 days of labels
choices.reason: Nightly retraining uses arriving labels and existing workflow tooling, but the requirements do not select Airflow or a 90-day window. The fixed window and full cadence deserve continued review as fraud adapts.
choices.solution_quote: An Airflow pipeline retrains the model every night on the last 90 days of labelled transactions.

choices.value_id: Experiment and promotion: Three-day shadow and manual review
choices.reason: A comparison before promotion follows Q4, but three days exceeds its deadline; a one-day shadow can fit the time bound, so this duration is not forced and fails the requirement.
choices.solution_quote: A new model first runs in shadow mode next to the production model for three days; the risk team reviews the comparison and promotes it by hand in MLflow.

choices.reason: The registry records model versions and training snapshots, but no requirement uniquely selects MLflow over another managed in-environment approach.
choices.solution_quote: MLflow records the parameters, the metrics, the training data snapshot and the model artifact of every run, and holds the model registry.

choices.value_id: Monitoring: Grafana score drift and fallback dashboards
choices.reason: Drift and fallback monitoring helps operators respond to changing fraud and service degradation, but the tools and dashboard choices are not prescribed by a requirement.
choices.solution_quote: Grafana dashboards show the score distribution and the share of rule-engine fallbacks, and alert when the score distribution drifts from last month's.

adrs.title: Maintain fresh online activity features
adrs.context: Each transaction must use the cardholder's recent activity before authorization. Seasonal throughput makes the feature read path latency-sensitive.

options.name: Streaming aggregates in Redis
pros: Keeps hour/day card aggregates current as events arrive.
Supports online reads for the transaction scoring path.
cons: Depends on Redis availability and capacity.
The 30 ms peak p99 is not established by this design description.
options.reason: Streaming is the better-supported match for per-transaction recent activity; Redis is a reasonable online store but its exact choice is free.

options.name: Batch recomputation
values: Feature state: Batch recomputation of recent card aggregates
pros: Can rebuild consistent aggregates and correct state.
cons: Can serve stale features between runs and create periodic processing load.
options.reason: It weakens the freshness required for recent activity and is less supportive of the low-latency scoring intent.

adrs.title: Score synchronously and preserve authorization continuity
adrs.context: The score must be available before the authorization decision, while a scoring outage or timeout must not prevent authorization.

options.name: Synchronous model score with rules fallback
values: Scoring path: Synchronous REST on Kubernetes
pros: Returns a model score on the authorization path.
A rules fallback lets authorization continue through scoring failures.
cons: The synchronous dependency can add latency and capacity pressure.
Fallback decisions may provide weaker fraud detection.
options.reason: Q2 forces a continuity path such as the rules fallback. Synchronous REST, Kubernetes, and XGBoost are implementation choices; the stated peak latency remains unverified.

options.name: Synchronous scoring with no fallback
values: Scoring path: Synchronous REST on Kubernetes
Failure behavior: No fallback on scoring failure
pros: Every completed decision comes directly from the model path.
cons: A service failure can stop the authorization flow.
options.reason: It misses Q2, which forbids an authorization failure caused by scoring.

adrs.title: Keep score explanations and replay evidence
adrs.context: Months after a transaction, the team must identify the model and values used, and answer with training lineage within one working day while card data stays in the PCI environment.

options.name: Return top features and retain complete score records
values: Score explanation: Top three contributing features
Audit record: Append-only full input and model log
pros: Complete score inputs and model version support replay and historical explanation.
Thirteen months covers the stated lookback.
Training snapshots and model artifacts preserve lineage.
cons: Full input retention consumes storage and requires careful access governance.
options.reason: The versioned input record, required retention and internal storage are forced by Q3 and C1. Top-feature output and MLflow are useful choices, but alternatives could satisfy the same requirements.

adrs.title: Retrain and compare candidate models
adrs.context: New confirmed cases must feed model updates, and a candidate must be compared on recent transactions and reach production within 48 hours. The seven-person team has no ML platform group.

options.name: Nightly Airflow training with three-day shadow and manual promotion
values: Retraining pipeline: Airflow nightly on 90 days of labels
Experiment and promotion: Three-day shadow and manual review
pros: Nightly jobs consume newly confirmed labels.
The shadow comparison and manual review limit exposure to a poor release.
The registry tracks parameters, snapshots and artifacts.
cons: Three days in shadow exceeds the 48-hour deadline.
Nightly scheduling and manual review still use scarce staff time.
A fixed 90-day window may omit useful older patterns.
options.reason: R2 supports regular retraining and Q4 supports comparison before promotion, but the chosen three-day duration is not forced and fails Q4. Airflow and MLflow are practical rather than mandatory tools.

options.name: One-day shadow with manual review
values: Experiment and promotion: One-day shadow and manual review
pros: Can compare the candidate with current production transactions within the 48-hour target.
Retains a human review gate and registry lineage.
cons: Shorter observation gives less evidence about varied fraud patterns.
Manual review still consumes team time.
options.reason: This shows that the three-day delay is not required by the comparison requirement; the requirements do not explain why the built system chose a delay that misses Q4.

adrs.title: Monitor drift and operational fallback
adrs.context: Fraud patterns change and the shared operations team needs visibility into degraded scoring and changing score behavior.

options.name: Grafana drift and fallback dashboards
values: Monitoring: Grafana score drift and fallback dashboards
pros: Shows fallback share and score distribution changes.
Alerts provide an operational signal for drift.
cons: Drift alerts do not themselves retrain or validate a model.
options.reason: This supports responding to changing fraud and service health, though the monitoring tool and thresholds are free choices and do not alone satisfy Q4's release deadline.
